verdict.rationale: The proposition bundles three claims and the lexicon answers them unequally. The identification of the baptized believer with Christ's death, burial, and resurrection is firmly grounded in the aorist passive forms parsed in the store: synetaphemen (G4916, V-2API-1P, Rom 6:4) and the participle syntaphentes with synegerthete (G4916, V-2APP-NPM, Col 2:12) set burial-with and raising-with at the center of the act, and synthapto occurs in only these two verses in the whole canon. The mode claim of full immersion is the contested element. The root verb bapto (G0911) means to dip (Luke 16:24, John 13:26, Rev 19:13), the brief lexicon glosses baptizo (G0907) as to dip, immerse, sink, baptisma (G0908) literally as immersion, and the descent-ascent narration of Acts 8:38-39 plus Mark 1:10 (katabaino, anabaino, ek, hydor) and the much-water note of John 3:23 cohere with immersion. But the same word group names ceremonial washings that need not submerge: baptizo of pre-meal hand washing (Luke 11:38) and baptismos (G0909) of rinsing cups (Mark 7:4) and of the various lustral washings of the law applied to flesh (Heb 9:10, Heb 6:2), while 1 Cor 10:2 calls Israel baptized in the cloud and sea without going under. No anchor or command text states the mode. Because the mode is lexically defensible but not lexically mandated, the bundled proposition is materially contested on mode while strong on the union symbolism and the faith confession.

scripture.force: Paul asks e agnoeite hoti hosoi ebaptisthemen eis Christon Iesoun eis ton thanaton autou ebaptisthemen, twice using the aorist passive of baptizo (the store parses it G0907, V-API-1P, we were baptized) with eis plus accusative goal. The construction frames baptism as incorporation into Christ and specifically into his death. This grounds the death-identification element of the proposition, but the clause speaks of the referent and effect of the act, union with the dying Christ, not of the physical mode of administering water.

synetaphemen oun auto dia tou baptismatos eis ton thanaton, hina hosper egerthe Christos ek nekron. The store parses synetaphemen as G4916 V-2API-1P, a 2nd aorist passive, we were buried with, and the following hina clause moves to walking in newness of life (kainoteti zoes) patterned on the resurrection. synthapto occurs in only two verses of the whole canon, this one and Col 2:12, so its sense is fixed by these baptism contexts. The burial-and-raising structure is the load-bearing image and matches a going-down and coming-up motion, the strongest lexical support for the immersion reading, though the figure is union with Christ rather than a stated rubric of submersion.

syntaphentes auto en to baptismo, en ho kai synegerthete dia tes pisteos pairs being co-buried in baptism with being co-raised through faith in the working of God who raised Christ from the dead. The store parses syntaphentes as G4916 V-2APP-NPM, a 2nd aorist passive participle, having been buried with. The explicit mention of faith (pisteos) supports the confession-of-faith element of the proposition, and the buried-and-raised pairing reinforces the death-burial-resurrection identification. Note that this verse is the one place the canon uses baptismos (G0909) of Christian baptism, the same noun used of Jewish lustral washings in Mark 7:4 and Heb 9:10. The verse describes meaning and instrument, not the geometry of how much water covers the body.

katebesan amphoteroi eis to hydor, ho te Philippos kai ho eunouchos, kai ebaptisen auton (ebaptisen parsed G0907 V-AAI-3S, he baptized). Both men go down (katabaino, G2597) into (eis) the water before the baptizing, and verse 39 has them come up (anabaino, G0305) out of (ek) the water, the same verbs confirmed token by token in the store. This eis and ek pair with verbs of descent and ascent is the narrative datum most consistent with immersion. It is suggestive but not decisive, since going down to and up from a body of water describes approach and departure and would also fit a baptism performed while standing in shallow water.

At the baptism of Jesus the store confirms anabainon ek tou hydatos, coming up out of the water, with G0305 anabaino, G1537 ek, and G5204 hydor present in the verse, the same descent-ascent vocabulary as Acts 8. This parallel narrative datum, where the one baptized comes up out of the water, strengthens the immersion-consistent reading, though here too the language describes the motion of the person relative to the water, not a prescribed quantity of water.

en de kai ho Ioannes baptizon en Ainon engys tou Saleim, hoti hydata polla en ekei. The store confirms baptizo (G0907) with hydor (G5204) and polys (G4183), much water, at Aenon. The note that much water was present coheres with the immersion reading, since immersion needs a sufficient body of water, but the clause states a circumstance of the location rather than a rule for the mode, so it supports without mandating.

idou hydor, ti kolyei me baptisthenai. The eunuch points to available water as the only stated prerequisite for being baptized, with the aorist passive infinitive baptisthenai (G0907). The text presents water plus the candidate's confessed readiness as sufficient and names no mode, which is neutral to the specific immersion claim while affirming that a body of water and a willing confessor are what the practice requires.

ho de Pharisaios idon ethaumasen hoti ou proton ebaptisthe pro tou aristou, where the aorist passive of baptizo (G0907) denotes the ritual washing expected before a meal, not a full-body submersion. The brief lexicon assigns this to sense 2 of the verb, to perform ablutions, wash oneself, bathe. This shows the verb itself can name a ceremonial washing short of immersion, which complicates the claim that the lemma by itself fixes the mode as full immersion in every context.

kai ap agoras ean me baptisontai ouk esthiousin, kai alla polla estin ha parelabon kratein, baptismous poterion kai xeston kai chalkion. The word group (baptizo G0907 and baptismos G0909) covers ceremonial washings of persons and of cups, pitchers, and kettles, items that were rinsed or sprinkled rather than necessarily plunged. The brief lexicon glosses baptismos here as a dipping, washing, lustration. This is the clearest lexical evidence that the noun and verb do not by themselves entail full immersion, the reason the mode element is contested rather than settled.

monon epi bromasin kai pomasin kai diaphorois baptismois, dikaiomata sarkos. The store confirms baptismos (G0909) used here of the various washings of the old covenant law applied to the flesh. Many of those washings in the law were performed by sprinkling or pouring (the cleansing rites of Leviticus and Numbers), so this verse shows the baptismos word denoting a class of purifications whose mode was not uniform submersion. It complicates any inference that the baptism vocabulary by itself prescribes immersion.

kai pantes eis ton Mousen ebaptisanto en te nephele kai en te thalasse. The store confirms baptizo (G0907) here with nephele (G3507, cloud) and thalassa (G2281, sea). Israel is said to have been baptized in the cloud and in the sea, yet the narrative has them pass through on dry ground while the cloud overshadowed and the sea stood as walls, so the people themselves were not submerged. This is a strong lexical complication: the verb can describe a water-and-cloud event of identification without literal submersion of the subjects, which blocks treating immersion as the necessary referent of baptizo.

I will sprinkle clean water (zaraq, H2236, confirmed in the store) upon you and you shall be clean. This prophetic purification, reached as an OpenBible cross-reference from the Acts 8:36 baptism scene, pictures cleansing accomplished by casting or sprinkling water onto the person rather than by submerging the person, and zaraq is one of the dominant purification verbs of the law (70 occurrences). It supplies an OT pattern of cleansing-by-application that the NT baptism vocabulary does not exclude, which is why the mode question is left open by the words.

Naaman went down and dipped (taval, H2881, glossed in the store to dip, dip into, plunge) seven times in the Jordan. The Septuagint renders this Hebrew verb with the middle of baptizo, providing the clearest pre-Christian bridge for the word, where the action is plainly a full dipping in a river. This supports the immersion sense of the verb at its lexical root, even though taval elsewhere can name a dip that prepares a sprinkling rite, as when hyssop is dipped in blood or water in Lev 14:6 and Num 19:18.

complicating_texts.resolution: The verb baptizo here names the pre-meal washing the Pharisee expected, a ceremonial ablution not requiring submersion (the brief lexicon places it in sense 2, to perform ablutions, bathe). This is addressed by distinguishing the semantic range of the lemma, which includes ritual washing, from its referent in the baptism texts. The complication does not overturn the union-with-Christ symbolism of Rom 6 and Col 2, but it does block the inference that the lemma alone mandates full immersion, which is why the verdict on mode is disputed rather than affirmed.

The application of baptizo and baptismos to washings of hands and of cups, pitchers, and kettles shows the word group covers acts performed by rinsing or sprinkling, not only by plunging. This is addressed by acknowledging that the lexical range is broad enough to admit non-immersive washing; the immersion reading therefore rests on the burial imagery of Rom 6 and Col 2, the descent-ascent narration of Acts 8 and Mark 1, and the root sense of bapto, rather than on the bare lemma, leaving the mode lexically defensible but not lexically required.

baptismos here labels the various washings of the law, many of which Leviticus and Numbers perform by sprinkling or pouring. This is addressed by noting that the same noun used of Christian baptism in Col 2:12 elsewhere covers a class of purifications whose mode is not uniform submersion, so the noun does not by itself fix immersion. It deepens rather than removes the contest on mode.

Israel is said to be baptized in the cloud and the sea while passing through on dry ground, so the subjects were not submerged. This is addressed by treating it as decisive proof that baptizo can describe an identifying water-and-cloud event without literal immersion of the persons, which is why the verb alone cannot carry the exclusive-immersion claim. The union and identification sense survives; the strict mode does not.

variants.note: All anchor verses lie in the New Testament outside 3 John, so CBGM data is not in scope for this run and not_in_ecm_scope is true. The apparatus sigla flagged in Col 2:12 (the baptismo versus baptismati reading, the noun form, and the ek marker) and in Acts 8:36 and 8:38 (the baptisthenai infinitive and the longer verse 37) touch the form of the baptism noun and minor wording, not whether the act involves burial-and-raising imagery or descent into water. The verdict holds across the plausible readings, so it is treated as variant robust.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Taking the root verb bapto (G0911), which means to dip, together with the brief lexicon gloss of baptizo as to dip, immerse, sink and of baptisma as immersion, the LXX bridge at 2 Kgs 5:14 where Naaman dips in the Jordan, the co-buried and co-raised aorist passives of Rom 6:4 and Col 2:12, the descent-and-ascent narration of Acts 8:38-39 and Mark 1:10, and the much-water note of John 3:23, yields affirmation of immersion as the fitting and likely mode, since burial and resurrection are best pictured by going under and rising from water. On this reading the strongest sense of the words and the strongest images point the same way.

Taking the full canon range of the word group, baptizo of pre-meal washing in Luke 11:38, baptismos of rinsing cups in Mark 7:4 and of the various lustral washings of the law applied to flesh in Heb 9:10 and Heb 6:2, and especially 1 Cor 10:2 where Israel is baptized in the cloud and sea without being submerged, yields a disputed verdict on mode. The verb covers cleansing accomplished by application as well as by dipping, the OT purification it echoes is often by sprinkling or pouring (Ezek 36:25, zaraq), and the texts that command baptism never specify a quantity of water. The death-burial-resurrection identification and the link to faith stand either way; only the exclusive mode is underdetermined. A reader holding this lens regards immersion as well suited and probably original but not lexically obligatory.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition is a bundle. Its identification clause (death, burial, resurrection) and its confession-of-faith clause are lexically supported by Rom 6, Col 2, and Acts 8, with synthapto occurring in only the two burial-baptism verses of the canon. Its mode clause (full immersion) is the part the lexicon underdetermines. The store can show that immersion is the root sense of the verb, that it fits the burial figure, and that descent-and-ascent language attends two baptism narratives, but it cannot show that the texts mandate immersion to the exclusion of pouring, because the same word group elsewhere names washings that are not submersions and one text (1 Cor 10:2) applies the verb where no one went under. progressive_revelation is set true because the OT dipping background (taval) and the OT sprinkling-cleansing promise (Ezek 36:25) both feed the NT vocabulary and pull in different mode directions.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Water baptism in the New Testament signifies union with Christ in his death, burial, and resurrection and is received upon confessed faith; whether the prescribed or normative mode of administering the water is full immersion as opposed to pouring or sprinkling is the question under test.
stem_audit.notes: The clause is administered by full immersion states the contested mode as a settled fact and so embeds the immersionist verdict into the stem. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized_form separates the lexically attested elements (union symbolism and faith confession) from the contested element (the exclusive immersion mode), so the disputed finding attaches specifically to the mode claim and not to the identification it bundles with. Verdict affirms is unchanged from the prior file (disputed); the deeper query confirmed both lenses with real data rather than forcing a flip.

lay_summary: The statement makes three claims at once: that baptism is done by full immersion, that it is a public confession of faith, and that it pictures the believer's identification with Christ's death, burial, and resurrection. The original-language evidence answers these unevenly. The death, burial, and resurrection part is on solid ground. In Romans 6 Paul says all who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death, and that we were buried with him through baptism so that we might walk in newness of life. Colossians 2 says the same, that we were buried with him in baptism and also raised with him through faith. The verb for buried with him appears in only these two verses in the whole canon, so its meaning is anchored right here, and the link to faith is explicit. So the union with the dying and rising Christ, and the role of faith, are clearly carried by the words. The immersion part is the disputed piece. The root verb behind baptize simply means to dip, and the standard lexicon gives the core sense of baptize as to dip, immerse, sink. In the Old Testament Greek the same verb describes Naaman dipping seven times in the Jordan. In Acts 8 Philip and the official both go down into the water and come up out of the water, the same down-and-up wording used when Jesus comes up out of the water in Mark 1, and John baptized at Aenon because there was much water there. All of this fits immersion well. But the same word family is also used for washings that did not require going under. A Pharisee is surprised Jesus did not first wash before a meal, the word covers the rinsing of cups and kettles, and Hebrews uses it for the various ceremonial washings of the law, many of which were done by sprinkling. Most tellingly, Israel is called baptized in the cloud and the sea even though they crossed on dry ground and were never submerged. Because the verb covers cleansing by application as well as by dipping, and because the texts that actually command baptism never state how much water is used, the picture of burial and rising favors immersion strongly but the words do not require it to the exclusion of pouring. For that reason the overall statement reads as genuinely contested on the question of mode, while its symbolism and its link to faith stand firmly.
